title: In Search of Excellence
author: Tom Peters, Robert H. Waterman Jr.
blurb: The 1982 bestseller that profiled America's best-run companies and boiled their success down to eight attributes, among them a bias for action and staying close to the customer.
why_not: The Skeptic's case: several of its excellent companies stumbled within a few years, which makes it the classic warning about reading success backward from survivors. That lesson lives on in The Halo Effect, which made the list.

title: The 33 Strategies of War
author: Robert Greene
blurb: Greene's compendium of military strategy recast as rules for everyday conflict, popular well beyond military readers.
why_not: The Mindset Coach nominated it, but the Professor and the Skeptic scored it 1: vivid stories, little evidence, and more about winning fights than building advantage.

title: Strategy Safari
author: Henry Mintzberg, Bruce Ahlstrand, Joseph Lampel
blurb: A tour of ten schools of strategic thought, from design and planning to learning and power, by Henry Mintzberg, a leading critic of strategic planning.
why_not: The Professor scored it 5 as the best map of the field. Everyone else found it a book about strategy theories rather than a way to make strategy, and the Mindset Coach scored it 1.

title: Sprint
author: Jake Knapp, John Zeratsky, Braden Kowitz
blurb: The five-day process from Google Ventures for going from a problem to a tested prototype, used by product teams worldwide.
why_not: It lost a 4 to 2 vote to Continuous Discovery Habits. The Modernist argued that when a prototype takes an hour, a five-day ritual compresses, while weekly customer contact gets more valuable.

title: The Soul of a New Machine
author: Tracy Kidder
blurb: Kidder's Pulitzer Prize-winning account of a Data General team racing to build a new computer, still a favorite among engineers.
why_not: It scored just below Hello World and lost the balance check to it. It is closer to narrative nonfiction than a framework, which the scope rule treats cautiously.

title: The Coming Wave
author: Mustafa Suleyman, Michael Bhaskar
blurb: A DeepMind co-founder's argument that AI and synthetic biology will be hard to contain, and that containment is the central problem of the century.
why_not: The Modernist scored it 5 as the most direct book on the stakes of AI. The Operator and the Mindset Coach scored it 2, finding little a reader can apply at work, and it was young for the canon.

title: Think and Grow Rich
author: Napoleon Hill
blurb: One of the best-selling self-help books ever, built on the promise that a burning desire and a definite purpose lead to wealth.
why_not: The Skeptic showed that Hill's claims about where his material came from can't be confirmed, and the Professor and the Modernist scored it 1. Its reach is real; its method is not testable.

title: Can't Hurt Me
author: David Goggins
blurb: A former Navy SEAL's memoir and challenge program for mental toughness, a long-running bestseller.
why_not: The Mindset Coach scored it 5. The Professor scored it 1 and the Skeptic 2: a memoir first, and Do Hard Things makes the evidence-based case for toughness that the panel preferred.

title: Inner Excellence
author: Jim Murphy
blurb: A performance coach's training program for the mind, drawn from work with elite athletes and blending Stoic, Eastern and psychological practice. Revised in 2020 and reissued by a major publisher in 2025.
why_not: Nominated by Joe. The Mindset Coach scored it 5, but it lost 4 to 2 because The Inner Game of Tennis already holds the coaching-the-mind slot with the original idea. It stays an alternate.
